w: Thomas Jefferson co-designed this statehouse in France, modeling it on the Maison Carree, the Roman temple at Nimes. Built 1785-1788, it houses the oldest elected legislative body in the Americas, dating to the 1619 House of Burgesses, and from 1861 to 1865 doubled as the Confederate capitol.
s: Jefferson's Roman-temple capitol, once Confederate too
_facts: Conceived by Thomas Jefferson and Charles-Louis Clerisseau, modeled on the Maison Carree in Nimes
Built 1785-1788, the eighth building to serve as Virginia's capitol
Houses the oldest elected legislative body in North America (House of Burgesses, 1619)
Served as the Confederate capitol 1861-1865; National Historic Landmark since 1960

w: Richmond's public history museum interprets the Holocaust through three strands: survivor testimony, artifacts, and educational programming. It centers lived memory over abstraction, pairing firsthand survivor accounts with period objects for visitors, students, and researchers.
s: Holocaust history told through survivor testimony
_facts: Public history museum in Richmond, Virginia
Dedicated to interpreting the history of the Holocaust
Uses survivor testimony, artifacts, and educational programming

w: Once a separate river port, Manchester shipped tobacco and coal from Midlothian via Virginia's first toll road (1807) and first railroad (1831). It was also a port of entry for slave ships. In 1910 it merged into Richmond, the earliest Virginia city to lose independence; a slave trail traces the route from the docks.
s: Former slave-ship port, now walkable Old Manchester
_facts: Former independent city on the James River's south bank, county seat of Chesterfield 1870-1876
Port of entry for slave ships, principally in the 18th century
Shipped tobacco and coal via Virginia's first paved toll road (1807) and first railroad (1831)
Merged into Richmond in 1910, the first Virginia independent city to do so; slave trail traces the route from the docks

w: One family paid for the whole cathedral: Thomas Fortune Ryan and his wife financed construction from 1903, the only cathedral known at the time built solely through one family's patronage. Completed in 1905, consecrated in 1906, it stands on North Laurel Street facing Monroe Park and hosts VCU's campus ministry.
s: The cathedral one family paid for outright
_facts: Seat of the Diocese of Richmond
Construction financed entirely by Thomas Fortune Ryan and his wife, 1903-1905
Completed 1905, consecrated November 29, 1906
Virginia Historic Landmark and National Register listing; hosts VCU's Catholic campus ministry

w: Richmonders call it the Birdcage: an ornate cast-iron cage designed by Albert Lybrock enclosing the tomb of President James Monroe in Hollywood Cemetery. His remains were moved from New York's Marble Cemetery in 1859, decades after his death, and the ironwork earned National Historic Landmark status in 1971.
s: The Birdcage: a president's iron-caged tomb
_facts: Burial place of President James Monroe in Hollywood Cemetery
Cast-iron cage designed by Albert Lybrock, installed 1859
Body moved from Marble Cemetery, New York City
National Historic Landmark since 1971; locally nicknamed the Birdcage

w: Patrick Henry stood inside this 1741 wooden church and closed his Second Virginia Convention speech with 'Give me liberty, or give me death!' Richmond's oldest church, built by Colonel Richard Randolph, lent its name to the surrounding Church Hill district and is now a National Historic Landmark.
s: Where Patrick Henry demanded liberty or death
_facts: Oldest church in the city of Richmond, built 1741 by Colonel Richard Randolph
Site of Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty or give me death' speech, Second Virginia Convention
Gave its name to the surrounding Church Hill district
Designated a National Historic Landmark

w: Built in 1818, this Court End mansion was Jefferson Davis's executive residence from August 1861 to the Confederacy's collapse in April 1865. The Confederate Memorial Literary Society ran it as a museum 1894-2014, before merging into the American Civil War Museum. Now on the VCU campus, a National Historic Landmark.
_facts: Built 1818 in the Court End neighborhood
Executive residence of Confederate President Jefferson Davis, Aug 1861-Apr 1865
Owned by the Confederate Memorial Literary Society 1894-2014, then merged into the American Civil War Museum
National Historic Landmark since 1960; now on the VCU campus

w: Eleven bronze women stand life-sized in a granite plaza on the Capitol grounds, from Pamunkey chieftain Cockacoeske to businesswoman Maggie L. Walker. First proposed in 2009, the plaza opened in 2018 with seven statues unveiled in 2019; four more joined in May 2022. StudioEIS of Brooklyn sculpted them all.
s: Eleven Virginia women, cast in bronze
_facts: Officially titled 'Voices from the Garden: The Virginia Women's Monument'
First proposed 2009, established by the General Assembly in 2010
Granite plaza opened October 2018; seven statues unveiled October 2019
Four more statues added May 2022, including Maggie L. Walker and Martha Washington; sculpted by StudioEIS

w: Richmond's oldest Catholic church was the diocese's cathedral from 1850 to 1906. After the Civil War its basement held services for a Black Catholic congregation, including Emily Mitchell, born into slavery in 1824, and Moses Marx, who drove a bishop's buggy at age twelve. That growth led to founding St. Joseph Church.
s: Where Richmond's Black Catholics first worshipped
_facts: Oldest Catholic church in Richmond, cathedral/diocese seat 1850-1906
Basement hosted a 13-member Black Catholic congregation after the Civil War
Congregants included Emily Mitchell (born into slavery in 1824) and Moses Marx
Growth of the congregation led to founding St. Joseph Church on Shockoe Hill; designated a pro-cathedral in 2020
